title: Present value, NPV and discount rates

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A contractor's spreadsheet values a project at $96.3k, treating every amount as paid at the end of its year. Your table runs numpy-financial's npv on the same yearly amounts at 8%. What does your table show for that project?

options.text: $96.3k, since both tools use the same amounts and the same rate
options.says: Same amounts and rate, but a different timing: the page shows a shift of every flow by one year changes the NPV by the factor 1 + r.

options.text: $104.0k, since your table discounts every amount one year less
options.says: Right: npf.npv does not discount its first value, so each amount is one year less discounted: 96.3 x 1.08 = 104.0.

options.text: $89.2k, since your table discounts every amount one year more
options.says: Wrong direction: npf.npv counts the first amount at t = 0, so it discounts less than the end-of-year convention, not more.

options.text: $96.3k plus the first amount, since only that amount is timed differently
options.says: Every amount moves one year, not only the first; the page shows the whole NPV dividing by 1.07 when all flows shift.

origin.section: NPV Adds Every Discounted Cash Flow, Counted From One Stated Date

questions.stem: At a planning rate of 6%, option K has NPV $410k and IRR 9%, and option L has NPV $520k and IRR 7%. Only one can be funded. Which does the page's rule fund, and why?

options.text: K, because its higher rate of return means it pays back sooner
options.says: Paying back sooner is what IRR describes; the page ranks by NPV at the chosen rate, where L adds more value.

options.text: K, because its IRR already includes the 6% cost of the money
options.says: IRR is computed without the organization's rate; it is the rate at which the project's own NPV is zero.

options.text: Neither, because the rankings by NPV and by IRR disagree
options.says: A disagreement is expected and is settled by NPV at the chosen rate; the page's clearing and undergrounding disagree the same way.

options.text: L, because it adds more value at the rate the planners use
options.says: Right: rank by NPV at the chosen rate; IRR measures speed of return, not value added.

origin.section: The Discount Rate Is the Price of Waiting, and It Can Reorder Projects

questions.stem: A refurbishment will save $2,000k, paid in 2047. At the start of 2027, at a 7% discount rate, roughly what is that saving worth?

options.text: About $517k, since twenty years at 7% leaves about a quarter
options.says: Right: the page's 20-year factor at 7% is 0.2584, so 2,000 x 0.2584 = 517.

options.text: About $833k, since twenty years at 7% adds 140% to the amount
options.says: That is interest without compounding; each year's interest earns interest, so the factor is 1.07^20, not 1 + 20 x 0.07.

options.text: About $2,000k, since a payment's worth is the same in any year
options.says: The page's first rule: money later is worth less now, by the discount factor.

options.text: About $1,000k, since twenty years at 7% halves the amount
options.says: At 7% the factor is about one half after 10 years (0.5083), not 20.

origin.section: A Dollar Later Is Worth Less Than a Dollar Now
